item.question: Draw two rectangles each having the following perimeters. (a): 26 cm; (b): 18 cm
steps_tex: The perimeter of a rectangle is $2 \times$ length $+ 2 \times$ breadth, so length $+$ breadth is half of the perimeter.
$(a)$ Half of $26$ is $26 \div 2 = 13$, so length $+$ breadth $= 13$.
Choose a length and a breadth that add to $13$: $8 + 5 = 13$ and $10 + 3 = 13$. Draw a rectangle $8\text{ cm}$ by $5\text{ cm}$ and another $10\text{ cm}$ by $3\text{ cm}$.
$(b)$ Half of $18$ is $18 \div 2 = 9$, so length $+$ breadth $= 9$.
Choose $6 + 3 = 9$ and $7 + 2 = 9$. Draw a rectangle $6\text{ cm}$ by $3\text{ cm}$ and another $7\text{ cm}$ by $2\text{ cm}$.
Check: $6 + 3 + 6 + 3 = 18$ and $7 + 2 + 7 + 2 = 18$. Your rectangles may be different.
item.answer_tex: Sample answer: $(a)$: $8\text{ cm}$ by $5\text{ cm}$ and $10\text{ cm}$ by $3\text{ cm}$; $(b)$: $6\text{ cm}$ by $3\text{ cm}$ and $7\text{ cm}$ by $2\text{ cm}$. Your answer may differ.

item.question: Find the area of your classroom floor in square meters. Take the help of your teacher to measure the length and breadth of the floor. What is the perimeter of the classroom floor?
steps_tex: Measure the length and the breadth of the floor with a measuring tape, in metres.
Area of the floor $=$ Length $\times$ Breadth, in $\text{square m}$. Perimeter $= 2 \times$ Length $+ 2 \times$ Breadth, in metres.
Sample answer with practice values: a floor $8\text{ m}$ long and $6\text{ m}$ broad.
Area: $8 \times 6 = 48\text{ square m}$.
Perimeter: $2 \times 8 = 16$ and $2 \times 6 = 12$, and $16 + 12 = 28\text{ m}$.
Check: $8 + 6 + 8 + 6 = 28$. Your answer may differ, because your classroom may be a different size.

item.question: All the sides of a rectangle are equal, that is, the case of a square. Think about a square whose sides are 5 units long. What are its area and its perimeter?
steps_tex: All the sides of a square are equal, so the length and the breadth are both $5\text{ units}$.
Area of a square $=$ Length $\times$ Length $= 5 \times 5 = 25\text{ square cm}$.
Perimeter of a square $=$ Length $+$ Length $+$ Length $+$ Length $= 4 \times$ Length.
$4 \times 5 = 20$, so the perimeter is $20\text{ cm}$.
Check: adding the four sides, $5 + 5 + 5 + 5 = 20$.

item.question: A rectangular lawn has an area of 72 square m and a length of 9 m. What is its breadth?
steps: Area = Length × Breadth, so 9 times the breadth is 72.
Find the breadth by dividing the area by the length: 72 ÷ 9 = 8.
Check by multiplying back: 9 × 8 = 72, which is the area.
The breadth is 8 m.

item.question: A rectangle is 20 cm wide. Its height is marked in two parts, 5 cm and 7 cm. Find the area of the rectangle.
steps: The whole height is the two parts added: 5 + 7 = 12 cm.
Area = Length × Breadth = 20 × 12 = 240 square cm.
Check by parts: the upper part has an area of 20 × 5 = 100 and the lower part has an area of 20 × 7 = 140.
100 + 140 = 240, the same area.

The area is $64\text{ square m}$ and the length is $16\text{ m}$, so $16$ times the breadth is $64$.

item.question: Five square tiles are placed like the letter L: 3 tiles in the top row and 2 more tiles below the left tile. Each tile side is 1. Find the perimeter. Then say what happens when one more tile is added at the end of the top row, and when one is added in the corner where the two arms meet.
steps: Count the outer edges of each tile. The left tile of the top row has 2 outer edges, the middle tile 2 and the right tile 3.
Of the two lower tiles, the upper one has 2 outer edges and the lowest has 3.
Add: 2 + 2 + 3 + 2 + 3 = 12. The perimeter is 12.
A tile added at the end of the top row touches the figure along 1 edge, so the perimeter becomes 2 more: 12 + 2 = 14.
A tile added in the corner where the arms meet touches 2 edges, so the perimeter stays 12.
Check: counting the outer edges again, one by one, gives 12.
item.answer: The perimeter is 12; one more tile at the end makes it 14, and one in the corner leaves it 12

item.question: Find the perimeter of the tiles.
steps_tex: Each side of a tile is $1$. The perimeter is the number of outer edges.
Count along the top: the $3$ tiles of the top row show $3$ outer edges.
Count down the right side of the top row: $1$ outer edge.
Count under the top row, along the two tiles on the right: $2$ outer edges.
Count the edge on the right of the lower tile and the edge under it: $1 + 1 = 2$ outer edges.
Count the left side of both tiles: $2$ outer edges.
Add: $3 + 1 + 2 + 2 + 2 = 10$. The perimeter of the tiles is $10$.
Check: $4$ tiles have $4 \times 4 = 16$ edges in all, and the $3$ places where tiles touch hide $2$ edges each, $3 \times 2 = 6$, so $16 - 6 = 10$.

item.question: Take turns and add tiles to the same figure till the perimeter becomes 24. The one who makes the perimeter 24 wins the game.
steps_tex: Start with the $4$ tiles from before: the perimeter is $10$.
Player $1$ rolls a $1$ and adds $1$ tile that touches the figure along $1$ edge. The perimeter becomes $2$ more: $10 + 2 = 12$, with $5$ tiles.
Player $2$ rolls a $6$ and adds $6$ tiles to the same figure, without moving any tile. The figure now has $11$ tiles.
Count the edges of $11$ tiles: $11 \times 4 = 44$.
$10$ places where tiles touch each hide $2$ edges: $10 \times 2 = 20$.
The perimeter is $44 - 20 = 24$.
Player $2$ has made the perimeter exactly $24$, so Player $2$ wins. Your game may go differently. Your answer may differ.
